title: Mrs. Jacky Wrenn — pioneer history
text:
MRS. JACKY WRENN.

Away back in the long ago, there lived a family of Smiths. There are many Smiths, but this particular Thomas Smith and wife lived in Pennsylvania and on Jan. 19, 1832, a bright little daughter was born to them. It is to this daughter, Jacky Smith, that we want to direct your attention for a while. This girl grew to womanhood and married James M. Wrenn in Stockton, Missouri. To this union were born two boys and three girls, and all went well with this happy family until the cruel hand of war in[vaded—] the ho[me and] led the father to the fro[nt to fi]ght for the cause he believ[ed] to be right. This left Mrs. Wrenn with a battle to fight also[,] that of rearing her little childre[n] and providing them with the necessaries of life. This was no easy matter and many times while brooding over her cares and thinking of her companion, not knowing whether he were dead or alive, she could not keep the tears from coursing down her cheeks. A few months before the war closed, she, with about a dozen other women decided that by coming to Texas they might be nearer their loved ones and, perhaps, see or hear from them often[er]. So they loaded their families and provisions in their ox wagons, and started on their long journey, without a man in the crowd.

After about [two] months out, they landed in F[annin] county and Mrs. Wrenn stopped on the old Mallory farm—known in later years as the Jo[e] Pritchett farm.

In about six months the war closed, her hus[band] came home and they mo[ved to] their farm just south of Savoy there Mr. Wrenn died in 1888.

For several [?] Mrs. Wrenn
